q: Which property is shown by a crystalline solid but not by an amorphous solid?
o: Melting gradually over a range of temperatures
x: Crystalline solids have long-range order, so all bonds break at one temperature and the melting point is sharp. Amorphous solids such as glass soften gradually over a range of temperatures.

q: Glassy solids are often called supercooled (frozen) liquids because they:
o: have only short-range order and soften over a range of temperatures
have a perfectly regular lattice throughout
are made of long chain molecules
x: Glass is cooled so fast that its particles lock in a liquid-like, disordered arrangement with only short-range order, so it has no sharp melting point. Long chain molecules describe polymeric solids instead.

q: Which of the following is a crystalline solid?
x: Sodium chloride has ions arranged in a regular repeating lattice. Glass and pitch are amorphous, and rubber is a polymeric solid.

q: In a crystal, the unit cell is:
o: the smallest group of particles which, repeated in three dimensions, builds up the whole lattice
the largest single crystal that can be grown
a single atom at the centre of the crystal
the space between two neighbouring atoms
x: The unit cell is the basic building block: repeating it in three dimensions generates the whole crystal lattice. A single atom alone does not carry the repeating pattern.

q: A solid has the same physical properties in every direction and no sharp melting point. It is most likely:
o: a single crystal of a metal
x: Amorphous solids lack long-range order, so they are isotropic and melt over a range of temperatures. Crystals, whether metallic, ionic or covalent, have sharp melting points and can be anisotropic.

q: Polymeric solids such as polythene and rubber are made of:
o: ions held in a regular three-dimensional lattice
long chain molecules formed by repeating small units (monomers)
separate atoms with a sea of free electrons
atoms arranged completely at random with no bonds
x: A polymer is a long chain built from many repeated monomer units, mostly carbon based, which gives polythene and rubber their flexibility. A lattice of ions describes ionic crystals such as NaCl.

q: The SI unit of stress is:
x: Stress = force/area, so its unit is N m⁻² (the pascal). 'No unit' belongs to strain, which is a ratio of lengths.

q: The greatest stress a material can bear and still return to its original length when the load is removed is called its:
x: Up to the elastic limit the deformation is fully recoverable. Beyond it, at the yield point, the material starts to deform plastically, so the yield stress is the tempting but wrong choice.

q: A force of 200 N stretches a wire of cross-sectional area 2 mm². The tensile stress in the wire is:
x: A = 2 mm² = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m², so stress = 200/(2 × 10⁻⁶) = 1 × 10⁸ Pa. Leaving the area in mm² gives 1 × 10² Pa; using 1 mm² = 10⁻³ m² gives 1 × 10⁵ Pa.

q: A wire 2 m long with cross-sectional area 1 mm² stretches by 1 mm under a load of 100 N. Young's modulus of the material is:
x: Y = FL/(AΔL) = (100 × 2)/(1 × 10⁻⁶ × 1 × 10⁻³) = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa. Leaving ΔL in mm gives 2 × 10⁸ Pa; forgetting the length of 2 m gives 1 × 10¹¹ Pa.

q: A steel wire (Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa) is 3 m long with cross-sectional area 1.5 mm². A load of 300 N is hung from it. The extension is:
x: ΔL = FL/(AY) = (300 × 3)/(1.5 × 10⁻⁶ × 2 × 10¹¹) = 900/(3 × 10⁵) = 3 × 10⁻³ m = 3 mm. Leaving out the length gives 1 mm.

q: Two wires of the same material carry the same load. Wire Q has twice the length and twice the diameter of wire P. The extension of Q compared with that of P is:
x: ΔL = FL/(AY) with A ∝ d², so ΔL ∝ L/d² = 2/2² = ½. Forgetting to square the diameter gives 'the same'; ignoring the length change gives one-quarter.

q: A material that breaks soon after its elastic limit, showing almost no plastic deformation, such as glass, is described as:
x: A brittle material fractures with little or no plastic region beyond the elastic limit. A ductile material such as copper shows a large plastic region and can be drawn into wires.

q: A wire (Y = 2 × 10¹¹ Pa) is under a tensile stress of 2 × 10⁸ Pa, within its elastic limit. The elastic energy stored per unit volume is:
x: Strain = stress/Y = 2 × 10⁸/2 × 10¹¹ = 1 × 10⁻³, so energy per unit volume = ½ × stress × strain = ½ × 2 × 10⁸ × 10⁻³ = 1 × 10⁵ J m⁻³. Forgetting the ½ gives 2 × 10⁵ J m⁻³.

q: Increasing the pressure on a liquid by 1 × 10⁷ Pa reduces its volume by 0.5%. The bulk modulus of the liquid is:
x: K = ΔP/(ΔV/V) = 1 × 10⁷/0.005 = 2 × 10⁹ Pa. Using 0.5 instead of 0.005 gives 2 × 10⁷ Pa; multiplying instead of dividing gives 5 × 10⁴ Pa.

q: Water has bulk modulus 2 × 10⁹ Pa. A 2-litre sample is put under an extra pressure of 4 × 10⁶ Pa. The decrease in its volume is:
x: ΔV/V = ΔP/K = 4 × 10⁶/2 × 10⁹ = 2 × 10⁻³, so ΔV = 2 × 10⁻³ × 2 × 10⁻³ m³ = 4 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 4 cm³. Using 1 litre instead of 2 gives 2 cm³.

q: A metal cube of side 10 cm has its bottom face fixed. A tangential force of 1000 N on the top face moves it 0.01 mm sideways relative to the bottom. The shear modulus is:
x: Shear stress = 1000/(0.1 × 0.1) = 1 × 10⁵ Pa; shear strain = 1 × 10⁻⁵ m/0.1 m = 1 × 10⁻⁴; G = 10⁵/10⁻⁴ = 1 × 10⁹ Pa. Taking the area as 0.1 m² (side not squared) gives 1 × 10⁸ Pa; 1 × 10⁵ Pa is only the stress.

q: For a wire, the force–extension graph is a straight line from the origin up to 40 N at an extension of 5 mm. The elastic energy stored at 40 N is:
x: Energy = area under the F-x graph = ½ F x = ½ × 40 × 0.005 = 0.1 J. Forgetting the ½ gives 0.2 J; leaving x in mm gives 100 J.

q: In an insulator, the energy gap between the valence band and the conduction band is:
o: large, so almost no electrons can reach the conduction band
zero, because the two bands overlap
about 1 eV, so some electrons cross at room temperature
absent, because an insulator has no valence band
x: An insulator has a full valence band separated from an empty conduction band by a large gap, so ordinary heating cannot lift electrons across. Overlapping bands describe a conductor; a gap of about 1 eV describes a semiconductor such as silicon.

q: Pure silicon is doped with a small amount of arsenic (a pentavalent element). The result is:
o: a p-type semiconductor with holes as majority carriers
an n-type semiconductor with holes as majority carriers
a p-type semiconductor with electrons as majority carriers
an n-type semiconductor with electrons as majority carriers
x: Each arsenic atom uses four electrons in bonds and donates its fifth, so free electrons are the majority carriers and the material is n-type. Mixing up 'n' with the dopant's valency is the common slip.

q: Which impurity added to pure silicon produces a p-type semiconductor?
x: Boron is trivalent: it leaves one bond incomplete, creating a hole, so it is an acceptor and gives p-type material. Phosphorus, antimony and arsenic are pentavalent donors that give n-type material.

q: As the temperature of a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor is raised, its resistance:
o: increases, because the atoms vibrate more
stays the same, because the band gap is fixed
increases, because the band gap becomes larger
decreases, because more electrons cross into the conduction band
x: Heating gives more valence electrons enough energy to cross the gap, creating more electron-hole pairs, so conductivity rises and resistance falls. 'Increases' is true for metals, the tempting mix-up.

q: A piece of n-type silicon, taken as a whole, is:
o: negatively charged only at high temperature
x: The extra free electrons come from neutral donor atoms, each of which becomes a fixed positive ion, so total positive and negative charge are equal and the crystal is neutral. Thinking 'n-type' means negatively charged is the usual mistake.

q: In a semiconductor, a hole:
o: is a vacancy left by a missing electron in a bond and acts as a positive charge carrier
is a free electron in the conduction band
is a positive ion that moves through the crystal
is a gap between two crystal grains
x: When an electron leaves a covalent bond it leaves a vacancy; neighbouring electrons fill it in turn, so the hole moves like a positive charge carrier. The donor ions are positive but fixed in the lattice, so they do not carry current.

q: Which of the following is a ferromagnetic material?
x: Iron, nickel and cobalt are ferromagnetic: their domains align strongly in a magnetic field. Aluminium is paramagnetic, and copper and bismuth are diamagnetic.

q: In a diamagnetic substance, the atoms:
o: have permanent magnetic moments that line up in domains
have permanent magnetic moments that line up weakly with an applied field
have no net magnetic moment because the electrons' magnetic moments cancel in pairs
have magnetic moments that stay aligned after the field is removed
x: In a diamagnetic atom the electron spins and orbits cancel in pairs, so there is no net moment, and an applied field induces only a weak opposing effect. Permanent moments lining up weakly describes paramagnetism; domains describe ferromagnetism.

q: When a ferromagnetic material such as iron is heated above its Curie temperature, it:
o: becomes diamagnetic and is strongly repelled
becomes paramagnetic because its domains break up
x: Above the Curie temperature thermal agitation destroys the alignment within domains, so the material loses ferromagnetism and behaves as a paramagnet. It does not become diamagnetic.

q: The core of a transformer should be made of a material whose hysteresis loop is:
o: of any shape, since loop area does not affect energy loss
x: The area of the hysteresis loop equals the energy lost as heat per cycle per unit volume, so a narrow loop such as that of soft iron keeps losses low. A wide loop with high coercivity suits a permanent magnet instead.

q: A material for a strong permanent magnet should have:
x: High retentivity means much magnetism remains when the field is removed, and high coercivity means a large reverse field is needed to destroy it, so the magnet stays strong; steel has both. Soft iron has low coercivity, so it loses its magnetism easily and suits electromagnets instead.

q: When a superconductor is cooled below its critical temperature:
o: its electrical resistance falls to zero
x: Below the critical temperature a superconductor has zero resistance, so a current can flow without energy loss. Above that temperature it behaves as an ordinary conductor with finite resistance.
